items.title: Go vs. Python for an LLM Gateway: What We Measured
items.story_key: story|title:go vs python for an llm gateway what we measured
items.content_excerpt: A reproducible benchmark of KTMS (Go) against LiteLLM Proxy (Python) and eight other self-hosted gateways on identical cloud hardware: added latency, time to first token, throughput, memory, CPU and startup time. Python is the language of machine learning, so most teams reach for a Python gateway first. We built Keystone. The Model Switchboard. (KTMS) , our self-hosted LLM gateway, in Go instead. A gateway doesn’t run models. It moves bytes between your services and model vendors, and that is a networking problem. “Go is lighter” is easy to say and hard to check, so we built a reproducible benchmark stand and ran KTMS against LiteLLM Proxy on identical hardware, then against eight more self-hosted gateways. This post walks through what we measured, the bug the stand found in our own code, and where the numbers stop. Python gateways such as LiteLLM run on FastAPI and Uvicorn. To use more than one core, they start several worker processes, because of the Global Interpreter Lock. Each worker loads its own copy of the interpreter, the vendor SDKs and the data models. A Go service is one process: the runtime schedules goroutines across all cores and shares one set of connection pools. The whole stand is open source in ktms/bench and reruns with one command. Terraform creates an isolated network and two VMs, the script runs the suite and then destroys everything. We ran the full suite twice. Latency, memory, CPU and maximum throughput agreed within about 10% between the runs for every gateway; LiteLLM’s p99 was the exception. The charts show the mean of both. Non-streaming requests at a steady 200 RPS against an upstream that answers instantly. KTMS adds about 0.6 ms at the median and about 1.1 ms at p99. LiteLLM adds about 8.5 ms at the median, and its p99 swung from 27 ms in one run to 229 ms in the other, so the mean in the chart is only a rough guide. Both gateways delivered every chunk of every stream. KTMS forwards the first token about 0.7 ms after it arrives from the upstream. LiteLLM takes about 160 ms. It doesn’t merge chunks: the whole stream just starts later, and finishes the same ~160 ms later. The offered rate climbs from 250 to 4,000 RPS in steps of 20 seconds, with a 10 ms upstream. A step counts as sustained when at least 95% of the offered rate gets through with fewer than 1% errors. KTMS kept up with every step, including 4,000 RPS, the highest we tested. Its p99 stayed at 13 ms up to 2,000 RPS (direct: 11 ms) and grew to 26–43 ms at 4,000 RP

items.title: Show HN: An open source repo to use your personal context with any agent
items.story_key: story|title:an open source repo to use your personal context with any agent
items.content_excerpt: The durable context about you and your work, like preferences, decisions and background, shouldn't live inside one AI app. Keep it in your own database and let any agent use it. Paste that into any coding agent. It walks you through the setup and does the typing for you. The durable, cross-cutting context that every tool should know, and that no single repo can hold. Your preferences and how you like to work, decisions and the reasons behind them, corrections, people and plans, and stable background on your products and projects. Code-specific context, status updates and to-dos stay in your repo, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md . Agents are told to leave them out of Memex. Memex is an MCP server that runs on your own Supabase project. Agents connect to it, and the instructions they follow are plain text in the repo. It creates the tables, deploys the server and connects itself. You approve the steps that need an account. An agent pushes what it knows that is worth keeping and pulls what the others learned, without duplicates. You decide, for each agent, what it may save. Search blends meaning with exact words, favors recent notes when you ask, and shows the current version of anything that was corrected. Ask any agent that can run scheduled tasks to keep you in sync. Say it once, and every morning it catches up on what your other agents saved and, if you choose, saves what it learned. Fetches what your other agents saved and gives you a short summary. Nothing is saved, so nothing needs approving. Your yes at setup is the standing approval. Each run it saves a few durable decisions, lessons and facts, and tells you exactly what it saved. Built so it stays safe while you're not watching. The server itself caps an unattended run at a small number of short notes (10 by default, and you can change it), skips anything that looks like a secret, skips repeats of what it already saved (or what you retracted), and tags every note it saves. Agents are told to leave out anything taken from web pages or emails. If a save was wrong, "retract what you saved this morning" hides those notes, and only those, and they can be restored. Nothing is ever deleted. A nightly job reads what you saved since the last run and organizes it. It never deletes or rewrites what you wrote. Everything it changes is logged and can be undone. items.title: Show HN: Atlas – Let AI agents use your Mac without taking over your screen
items.story_key: story|title:atlas let ai agents use your mac without taking over your screen
items.content_excerpt: Atlas gives your agent a hidden second desktop on your Mac. It opens apps, clicks and types there while you keep working on yours. Your agent’s desktop, in the tools you already use. Pick a harness and try a task. “Find a free hour on Thursday afternoon and add a launch review to my calendar.” One command, then the usual macOS prompts. Atlas sets up a hidden desktop on your Mac. Ask your agent for something and get back to your work. Your screen, mouse and keyboard stay yours. Open Atlas to see your agent on its own desktop, clicking through your app and taking screenshots. Bring what the task needs. Atlas can copy a build, sample files or settings into the helper, then clean up after the task. Ask in plain language. Your agent opens apps, clicks controls by name, types and brings back screenshots. Every screenshot and every page of instructions fills your agent’s context. Here is what the same three tasks took through Atlas and through each agent’s own Computer Use, on the same model. Computer Use looks at the whole screen after every step, so a form with five fields took up to 153 screenshots. Codex’s Computer Use reads apps as text, so it took no screenshots and finished a little sooner. With Atlas, Codex took about two a task. Most of the context gap is instructions: about 6k tokens, against 2k for Atlas. Tokens of context each task added, median of three runs, on a MacBook Pro. Claude: Claude Code with Atlas, and Anthropic’s computer-use tool ( computer_toolset_20260801 , set up as its documentation describes) driving the same apps in the same helper. Codex: Codex with Atlas, and Codex’s own Computer Use on the desktop. Tokenizers differ, so each card has its own scale: compare bars within a card, not across them. A computer-use loop that takes fewer screenshots would cost less. The helper is a real macOS login on your Mac. Here is how it shares your Mac, and what it costs. When your agent finishes, it quits every app it opened and leaves the helper quiet, so nothing sits in memory for no reason. Until the next task, Atlas does nothing. Agents queue for the helper: one acts, the others are told Atlas is busy and wait their turn. Take Control puts you ahead of all of them. So it never drains your battery for nothing: watch live, every 5 seconds or paused, Stop holds every agent, atlas close --all quits what they opened and atlas logout signs the helper out. items.title: How big is the open model economy today?
items.summary: Our first open model economy research note for paid subscribers.
items.story_key: story|title:how big is the open model economy today
items.content_excerpt: My longest running agent testbed has been building the Interconnects Dashboard — an aggregator of all of the best data on open model adoption and performance from across the web. This dashboard is freely available and becoming quite useful. Still, all the measurements we have on open model adoption are incredibly imprecise. We have noisy platform metrics, marketing-related metrics from startups, and imperfect public evaluations. It takes an informed eye to figure out where things are going. These research notes are my current best approximations of where we stand. As with most things on Interconnects, our goal is to build well more value than we capture, so the data on the dashboard will remain free for the foreseeable future. These notes will be more raw than many of my articles, a place for sharing what I’m mulling over but don’t have complete evidence for (yet). They will be primarily paid, enabling me to speak more freely. If you work in AI policy or policy-facing research, please reach out to us and we can likely get discounted or free access. The primary question I wanted to address today is: What is the market for open model inference? Is it growing? Is it a rounding error relative to OpenAI/Anthropic? I’ve been building the best measurements I can here, primarily using the open model inference startups Baseten, Fireworks, and Together AI as the bellwethers here (along with the open model share of OpenRouter’s token volume, which they thankfully report in their API). The hyperscalers also likely have a major footprint here, e.g. Amazon Bedrock and Azure’s model garden, but I haven’t seen them break down usage by model category. The startups’ fates are much more directly correlated with the success of open model inference as a category. For the latest data, we can start with a slide from my talk on the open model economy (recording here ). These are the public disclosures from the open model startups on their token volume, over time, log-scale. This shows near-exponential growth, before the uptick that would follow GLM 5.2’s step change in open agents . For example, Fireworks announced at their first company conference this week that they’re serving more than 40T tokens per day to customers’ customized models. This is just one slice of their inference, a vertical that they said grew over 2x from this summer, so I would expect their total number this fall to be well above 100T tokens when we get the next update. items.title: vLLM Delivers Day-0 Support for Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.summary: vLLM supports Kimi K3.1 Pro on day 0: sparse attention on a KDA hybrid, a packed KV cache with FP8 or NVFP4 latents and MXFP4 index keys, token-sharded prefill, decode context parallelism, and fused low-latency decode.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:3.1|variant:pro|title:vllm delivers day 0 support for kimi k3 1 pro
items.content_excerpt: Kimi K3.1 Pro is Moonshot AI's most capable open-weight model: a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context that matches the strongest closed-source models on coding, agentic and knowledge benchmarks. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Figure 1: Sparse attention (DSA) in Kimi K3.1 Pro. The indexer scores every past token, keeps the top 2,048, and every query head attends exactly over only those tokens' latents. Step through it. The index keys are a second per-token cache next to the MLA latent. Under tensor parallelism (TP) both are replicated on every GPU; KDA state is per request, as in K3. The latent and the index keys can be quantized independently. An NVFP4 latent alone already brings K3.1 Pro below K3 with FP8. Opt-in MXFP4 index keys fit 11% more tokens on top and make the indexer 10–20% faster at long context. With both, eight GB300 GPUs hold 1.7× as many tokens as with FP8, and DCP8 multiplies that by seven: about 36 full 1M-token contexts at once, against 3 for TP8 with FP8. Figure 2: Measured KV cache capacity on 8× GB300. Change the latent and index-key formats, the parallelism, or the context length to see how many full contexts fit. Each DSA layer stores two per-token caches of different widths: the MLA latent (576 bytes in FP8, 352 in NVFP4) and the index keys (132 bytes in FP8, 68 in MXFP4). Neither width is a multiple of the other. The 69 KDA layers each add a recurrent state per request that is much larger than one layer's page of tokens. items.title: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
items.summary: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.

items.title: Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out
items.story_key: story|title:dharma field extractor any document in structured fields in json out
items.content_excerpt: A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost. In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE , a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task. OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing. However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record. Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database. A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem. So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning. Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. items.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
items.summary: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

items.story_key: story|title:the enterprise case for open weight models on databricks
items.content_excerpt: A thought-piece on how Unity AI Gateway and Omnigent combine lower costs, data sovereignty, operational autonomy, and model flexibility to meet the changing demands of enterprise AI strategy. by Jay Palaniappan , Elise Gonzales , Tanner Waggoner , Toby Messinger and Will Middlebrook As field engineers at Databricks, we spend our days inside enterprise AI deployments, where we’ve observed a clear shift in strategy. After two years of standardizing on single frontier model providers, companies are reevaluating their approach due to seven key pressures: 1. Spend is not generating sufficient returns. AI budgets have outpaced revenue and cost savings, prompting a need for better unit economics [1]. 2. Model rankings have changed repeatedly since 2023. The best model for coding, reasoning, and extraction changes month to month, and the top intelligence ranking has changed hands 20+ times since May 2023 [2] . Architectures tied to a single provider make it harder to adopt a better model as rankings change. 3. Frontier guardrails can block legitimate work. Model guardrails imposed by AI labs can refuse legitimate tasks, such as analyzing live malware or reproducing an exploit to patch it, a limitation discovered in the recent Hugging Face incident [6] [7] . When Hugging Face responders fed real attack logs and exploit payloads to hosted frontier models for analysis, the guardrails refused, and the team ran the analysis on an open-weight model (GLM 5.2) instead. 4. Data retention policies have evolved and may continue to do so. Some frontier providers have deviated from zero-data-retention (ZDR) policies, such as the 30-day minimum retention introduced with Anthropic's frontier tier [8] . For enterprises whose compliance policy was written around the principle that "no prompt or completion is ever stored," an upstream policy change could introduce problems and potentially require a system change. 5. Companies want visibility into and control over model governance. Demand is growing for end-to-end visibility and governance across AI models. Customers want searchable records of model inputs, outputs, errors, and agent actions to enable teams to evaluate accuracy and improve performance, as well as centralized controls to protect sensitive data and intellectual property. 6. items.title: See the agents, set the terms: new visibility and control for personal agents
items.summary: Personal AI agents have changed how users interact with the web, blurring the lines between automated and human traffic. Learn how Cloudflare gives site owners visibility and control to manage personal agent access.
items.story_key: story|title:see the agents set the terms new visibility and control for personal agents
items.content_excerpt: Personal agents are the intermediary between humans and the Internet, turning a person’s instructions into requests and actions on websites. A customer might ask a personal agent to compare products across your site, find support articles, or complete a purchase. To a site owner, all three interactions show up as automated traffic — and without a clear view of which agents are visiting and what they are doing, it can be difficult to know whether that traffic is helping your business or creating risk. Blocking agents altogether can feel like the safest choice, but it can mean losing customers. Better visibility into agent activity allows you to decide what access makes sense for your site. Today, we’re launching new analytics to help you understand how personal agents access your site on behalf of humans, along with more granular access policies to put those decisions into practice. Together, they let you welcome agents on your own terms, and in ways that support your business. Knowing which agent is behind a request turns unexplained automated traffic into traffic you can act on with confidence. Cloudflare maintains the largest verified bot directory in the world, and we are now bringing that intelligence into your traffic details. In Security Analytics, the Bot Analysis chart now shows Personal Assistants as a new category, next to Verified Bot, Likely Human, Likely Automated, and Automated. Security teams can select it to see only personal agent traffic over time. In Top statistics, a new Personal Assistants widget lists which agents are visiting your site and how many requests each one sends. Filter on one agent and every other widget updates to show only its traffic details: the paths it requests, the status codes it receives, and the networks it comes from. At a glance, you can see whether an agent is logging in, reading your product pages, reaching your checkout, or hitting errors on pages it cannot use. For sites that protect user accounts with Account Abuse Protection (currently in early access), site owners and fraud teams are able to see which user each agent represents. items.title: Article: Systemic Approach to Memory, Knowledge, and Context in Agentic AI Architectures
items.summary:
The article argues that reliable agentic AI architecture depends on a context engine that selects, injects, compresses, and expires information before it reaches the model. It separates context, memory, and knowledge, and recommends tiered memory, curated knowledge, and token budgeting. It also covers common anti-patterns, such as context stuffing and stale data loops, with mitigations.

By Adi Polak

items.title: claude-code v2.1.314
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
  • Added an optional groups list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too
  • Added guardrail_trace to Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, to log which Amazon Bedrock guardrail filter fired on a request, without the matched text
  • Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
  • Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
  • Fixed claude -p exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
  • Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and /compact with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
  • Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
  • Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's tool_reference blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
  • Fixed TLS connections failing with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
  • Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out
  • Fixed claude mcp logout reporting success when the MCP sign-in was not removed, for example while the macOS keychain is locked over SSH
  • Fixed extra sign-in renewals when several sessions share an Anthropic profile login and the credentials lock is busy
  • Fixed claude ultrareview and claude remote-control asking the workspace trust question in a CI job that has a terminal; with CI set they now refuse an untrusted folder at once
  • Fixed an administrator's TLS trust settings in managed settings not being applied in Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed model switching being refused on machines with managed plugin settings when one of your own --plugin-dir or --plugin-url plugins had a broken manifest or failed to download
  • Fixed the Bedrock and Vertex model upgrade offer coming back at every start when managed settings pin the model
  • Fixed forceRemoteSettingsRefresh set only in remote managed settings no longer applying once the stored copy had expired, which let sessions start without policy when the server could not be reached
  • Fixed "Continue automatically at usage limit" continuing more than three times without a prompt from you when a task restarted itself between waits (a /goal check-in, a background or scheduled task)
  • Fixed background and cloud sessions started with Ultracode turning it back on at their next start after it had been switched off
  • Fixed the last broken reply and its retry prompts staying in the conversation after Claude gave up on a tool call that could not be parsed
  • Fixed a PreCompact hook with very large output making compaction fail or repeat; each hook's output is now cut at 10,000 characters
  • Fixed background diff refreshes briefly taking the repository's index lock, which could make a git command run at the same moment fail with "Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists"
  • Fixed markdown tables jumping between grid and stacked layouts on half-typed rows while streaming, and long tables falling back to raw pipes
  • Fixed the /resume picker showing the text of CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md as a session's title when the session only ran slash commands
  • Fixed /btw answering from the main conversation when asked from a subagent's open transcript
  • Fixed pasting an image over SSH to a Linux machine doing nothing silently; the prompt now says to copy the file over and paste its path
  • Fixed claude remote-control sessions that failed to start when the session service was slow for a moment: the worker's registration is now retried with growing waits
  • Fixed model switches over Remote Control that take over 8 seconds getting a "still pending" error instead of the final result
  • Fixed the sandbox.excludedCommands setting description saying listed commands always run outside the sandbox; it now says every command in a call must match an entry
  • Fixed shell and MCP calls that auto mode, a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook blocked, or that otherwise did not run, reading as if they ran in a collapsed tool group
  • Fixed sandbox protections not applying to a worktree entered by claude -p --resume or --continue
  • Fixed hooks matching Bash not running on shell commands started by the Monitor tool; such hooks can block or ask, but not approve or rewrite those commands
  • Fixed a settings file excluded with --setting-sources still supplying some settings, such as auto mode rules and saved permission consents
  • Fixed auto mode reporting a call as blocked, and listing it in /permissions, when its safety check gave no verdict
  • Fixed a Claude apps gateway Vertex upstream hanging for minutes when a Google token endpoint accepts the connection and never answers
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway's start-up warning for a deprecated Claude Desktop key that it still serves as written saying "stops being accepted" after the key's end date
  • Fixed /upgrade opening the browser and starting a new login for plans billed through the App Store or Google Play; it now says where to change the plan
  • Fixed --resume, and rewinding past a switch to another model after a refusal, moving a session on a model name Claude Code doesn't recognize to a different model
  • Fixed requests failing when a gateway or cloud provider refuses one of Claude Code's beta headers by name: the request is sent again without it
  • Fixed model IDs spelled with a dot behind an LLM gateway, such as claude-opus-4.8, being treated as an older model with the wrong context window, output limit, effort, thinking mode and cost
  • Fixed Remote Control clients showing a stray "Compacted (ctrl+o to see full summary)" row after /compact
  • Fixed the cloud sessions tip and the Remote Control idle notice showing when an organization's policy turns those features off
  • Fixed a resumed claude.ai cloud session making a model call nobody asked for when the previous worker stopped just after receiving a new chat's files
  • Fixed WebFetch in Cowork cloud sessions silently dropping a PDF's text past 100,000 characters; it now says how much was unread and where to read on
  • Fixed Claude being told only that a command was declined after you stopped it with Esc or Stop in a cloud session or the IDE; it now also hears that the command may have run
  • Fixed blank lines at the top of a code block disappearing when the code block opens a quote
  • Fixed a blank line appearing above some ⎿ rows in the transcript view (Ctrl+O)
  • Fixed vim mode dw, dW, yw and yW carrying on past the end of the line, and made w and W stop on empty lines
  • Fixed x and Enter in the agent panel sometimes acting on the wrong agent when another agent started or finished
  • Fixed pasted text and dragged-in files being lost in Claude's question dialog unless the "Other" row had focus
  • Fixed pasted text being lost when a row in the prompt footer was selected
  • Fixed vim mode p over a character selection ignoring whether the yanked text was whole lines
  • Fixed vim mode aw and iw taking the line break at the end of a line
  • Fixed ↓ selecting footer items hidden by the ? help menu, the command list or a paste hint
  • Fixed Esc on a command's panel, such as /btw, also interrupting the subagent whose transcript is open
  • Fixed the welcome header in fullscreen mode showing the session's model while viewing a subagent or teammate that runs on a different model
  • Fixed the fullscreen transcript being left mid-conversation after "Restore conversation" in the rewind menu while scrolled up
  • Fixed a rare case where a deleted session could reappear in the resume list as an almost empty entry
  • Fixed prompts containing tags such as <bash-stdout> or <local-command-stdout> not being acknowledged to a local stream-json host
  • Fixed sessions staying untitled when the first prompt failed (for example on a usage limit) and the conversation continued afterward
  • Fixed the skill file watcher checking every removed skill kept in ~/.claude/skills/.trash, which added file system load that grew with each removal
  • Fixed the session name from /rename disappearing while Claude asks for permission or a plan decision, so side-by-side sessions stay identifiable
  • Fixed background sessions that fail to start being reported as a deleted daemon binary when the binary is still on disk
  • Fixed the tip and idle reminder about push notifications appearing when the push settings in /config are hidden or your organization has turned off Remote Control
  • Fixed ~/.claude/skills/.trash and ~/.claude/plugins/.trash growing without limit: each now holds about 1024 entries, whatever cleanupPeriodDays says
  • Fixed the Bash edit diff listing a whole file as changed when a CRLF file under git's line-ending conversion was re-saved unchanged or had one line edited
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an idle session moving to another runner instead of pausing when the runner's request to pause it lost its connection before Anthropic answered
  • Improved memory use in long headless and SDK turns that run many subagents: the parent session no longer keeps each subagent's tool results until the turn ends
  • Improved prompt history: Ctrl+R now matches text inside collapsed [Pasted text] pills
  • Improved the /design-sync upload prompt to show the folder, the project and the files it will upload or delete
  • Improved /permissions review tab, now called Recently blocked: the footer says what Esc will do with marked rows
  • Improved auto mode's blocked calls: messages name the command, say Claude may retry and auto mode checks again, and point to /permissions to review
  • Improved permission prompts: a long reason takes fewer rows, so it pushes the command being approved off the screen on fewer terminals
  • Improved the cloud session error shown while a request refused for your claude.ai login is still being retried: it now also suggests claude auth login
  • Improved the behavior of stored claude.ai, Team, and Enterprise logins when MDM and remote settings differ on base URL or apiKeyHelper
  • Improved /config in agent view to say how to stop agent view opening by default
  • Improved session auto-titles: a session that starts with a skill or a prompt-based command such as /security-review now gets a title from it instead of staying untitled
  • Improved --resume speed and memory use on damaged transcripts
  • Improved /context speed in sessions with ten thousand or more MCP tools
  • Self-hosted runner: Improved the error shown when a session's branch isn't on the git remote: it now covers a never-pushed branch, says how to fix each case, and no longer suggests retrying
  • Updated the /claude-api skill: its Datadog setup for API tracing now sends the dd-llmobs-enabled: true header, as the Console does, and its ant install instructions drop the outdated macOS xattr step
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to advise printing y-axis tick labels in full under 10,000, and horizontal ones in full under a million where they fit
  • Updated the bundled dataviz skill to answer donut and pie chart requests with ranked bars or a segmented bar that prints its values
  • Changed Claude's file tools to ask before editing the local copy of your organization's server-managed settings, as they do for your settings files
  • Changed /ultrareview to check workspace trust before it runs git, as claude ultrareview does
  • Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited which alias or function and to stop passing exported which/unsetenv functions to commands, so which is the system command or zsh builtin
  • Changed /permissions Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show
  • Changed auto mode in Cowork cloud sessions: a hook's allow of an MCP tool call now counts as no answer, so the classifier or a permission prompt decides
  • Changed hook if conditions such as Monitor(tail *) to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as Bash(tail *) matches Bash's
  • Changed the claude-api skill to ask to read a Managed Agents workflow run's workflow before changing the agent to improve that run
  • Changed flagged requests to retry on another model, not end in a refusal, when ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, availableModels or deniedModels leaves only an older Opus model, or none
  • Changed idle compaction to also run for subscribers with telemetry turned off, and on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and LLM gateways once the one-hour prompt cache is on
  • Changed FORCE_HYPERLINK=false (also no and off) to turn hyperlinks off instead of on
  • macOS: Changed git grep in most commands that Claude runs to use the C locale, to avoid a reported memory leak in macOS's regex library on files that aren't valid UTF-8
  • [VSCode] Fixed "Clear authentication" for MCP servers reporting success when the saved sign-in could not be removed
  • [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run
  • [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew
  • [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat
  • [VSCode] Changed CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved scheduled tasks: runs in Anthropic's cloud now load the plugins enabled on your claude.ai account
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved cloud session transcripts: a rename row now names the new title, and repository and environment lists show as a table instead of one line of JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed cloud sessions from the web, desktop and mobile apps to start even when a setup script exits with an error, instead of failing to start
  • [Remote Control] Fixed the permission mode button in Remote Control sessions showing the wrong mode until you typed; while your computer is online it now shows the real mode on open
  • [Claude Tag] Added a dismissible link to the Claude Tag API docs on the Bundles and Channels tabs in admin settings, for Enterprise organizations with Slack connected
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed @Claude !restart giving up after one failed workspace check in channels shared across Enterprise Grid workspaces; it now retries, then asks you to run it again
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a second confirmation DM and channel note when you connect your Claude account from Slack twice from the same link within a few minutes
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed follow-up messages in Slack showing no sign of progress while Claude's session waits for a self-hosted runner; Claude now posts a wait notice in the thread
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude sometimes not answering a tag in its own thread in Slack Connect channels where both organizations have installed Claude
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Retry on plugin and skill pages in Claude Tag admin settings discarding unsaved access changes after a failed load; your edits now stay in place
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed the repositories control in Claude Tag admin settings showing the same action twice; its menu now lists only what the button doesn't already do
